overview: The Chahamanas, commonly called Chauhans, became an important power around Shakambhari, Ajmer and the Delhi region. This card focuses on the Shakambhari-Ajmer ruling line, especially its twelfth-century prominence. The map’s approximate 600-1200 dates are not a securely documented imperial lifetime. Its broad outline even leaves Ajmer just south of the polygon and should not be read as a reliable boundary. Other Chahamana branches had their own histories.

periods.title: Kings recorded in stone
periods.summary: The Harsha inscription of 973 preserves a royal genealogy; it is an attestation, not a founding date.

periods.title: Twelfth-century regional power
periods.summary: Chahamana rulers competed with neighbouring kingdoms while supporting major building and literary projects.

periods.title: Conquest and later Chahamana rule
periods.summary: Prithviraj’s defeat in 1192 ended his power at Ajmer. A different Chahamana kingdom at Ranthambhor survived until 1301.

sections.title: A regional power with a long family history

items.text: The Harsha inscription of 973 lists ancestors of King Vigraharaja II. A longer genealogy at Bijolia in 1170 reaches back to a reputed founder, Samanta, and forward to Somesvara. Comparing these dated records helps historians build a chronology without treating every remembered ancestor as a securely dated ruler.

Expansion brought the Chahamanas into competition with the Chaulukyas of Gujarat to the west and the Gahadavalas farther east. Their kingdom belonged to a crowded political world of neighbouring courts and armies. Prithviraj’s later fame can make that wider contest easy to overlook.

The Jinmata pillar records of 1140 name Arnoraja with imposing royal titles. Yet the recorded building work was paid for by local patrons. These stones put a king’s authority and a family’s practical contribution together in one public document.

At Harsha, kings and their officers donated villages to a temple, while other people contributed fields. Religious institutions drew support from several levels of society. A public list of gifts preserved local contributions alongside the names of rulers.

Salt merchants from Shakambhari promised a small payment for each measure they sold, and northern horse traders contributed for each horse. The 973 Harsha record therefore links a hilltop sanctuary with everyday buying and selling, from salt measured out for customers to valuable animals changing hands.

The teacher Allata’s pupil Bhavadyota completed a garden, well and stone cistern for cattle at Harsha. Garden plants needed watering, and animals needed somewhere to drink. The same project joined worship, gardening and animal care. Even cattle had a place in the construction plan.

The Harsha inscription remembers the craftsmen Candasiva and his father Virabhadra. Their names let us glimpse a family behind the stonework. Pious donors also supplied funds and fields, so the monument’s history includes artisans and local supporters as well as ascetics and kings.

Two brothers, Alhana and Delhana, sons of Udayaraja, funded renovation at Jinmata in 1140. In 1174 Alhana appears again, repairing the temple hall. One person’s support stretched across 34 years and several reigns: buildings needed returning patrons as well as impressive opening ceremonies.

Arnoraja commissioned Ana Sagar, an artificial lake at Ajmer, in the middle of the twelfth century. This was an achievement in shaping the city’s water landscape. The gardens and white pavilions familiar to visitors today include much later Mughal additions; they do not all belong to the Chauhan court.

A Jinmata inscription dated 29 April 1140 ends with “मङ्गलं महाश्रीः” (maṅgalaṁ mahāśrīḥ), meaning “Bliss! Great prosperity!” This Sanskrit blessing was carved in Nagari script, shown here in modern Devanagari and normalized transliteration. Its warm closing follows the practical record of a temple renovation.

Vigraharaja IV was also associated with literary learning at Ajmer. The site now called Adhai Din Ka Jhonpra is identified with a Sanskrit college he commissioned, later transformed into a mosque. This evidence concerns a particular learned institution; it does not establish schooling for every child.

A stone inscription dated 22 November 1153 preserves part of Vigraharaja’s play Harakeli-nataka. The surviving scene includes Shiva, his wife Gauri, a jester and a doorkeeper. The record names its engraver, Bhaskara. Courtly literature could be playful, and a script could survive on a very heavy page.

In 1875-1876, inscribed basalt tablets were recovered from the courtyard at Adhai Din Ka Jhonpra. Fragments preserved two plays, including Somadeva’s Lalita-Vigraharaja-nataka honouring the king. Broken building material recovered voices from a literary world otherwise much harder to hear.

The later mosque reused carved material from Hindu and Jain temples and added Islamic inscriptions and architectural forms. Reading its different layers helps distinguish twelfth-century Chahamana work from construction after conquest. A surviving column and the building around it can belong to different chapters of history.

Prithviraj defeated Muhammad of Ghur in 1191 but lost to him in 1192. The reversal broke his political power. Remembering both encounters explains why his reign became so significant without imagining that one victory had permanently removed the kingdom’s military dangers.

Stories about Prithviraj changed for centuries. Historian Cynthia Talbot follows more than 800 years of retelling, showing how a ruler became a hero for different audiences. The familiar label “last Hindu emperor” belongs to later memory; it is not evidence that all Hindu kingdoms ended with him.

Chahamana rule continued elsewhere after Ajmer’s defeat. Hammir Chauhan ruled at Ranthambhor until Ala al-Din Khalji defeated him in 1301. That was a later kingdom with its own history, not proof that Prithviraj’s realm or the atlas polygon survived unchanged.

ending.text: Prithviraj’s defeat by Muhammad of Ghur in 1192 ended his rule at Ajmer. It did not erase Chahamana families or Rajasthan’s communities. Other branches continued, including the Ranthambhor kingdom defeated in 1301. The atlas cutoff at 1200 is therefore neither the precise conquest date nor the end of every Chauhan lineage.
